props.title: Uranium Drive-In

sections.content: **Uranium Drive-In (2013)** (2013) offers a stark look at the complex intersection of environmental concerns and economic survival in rural America. Director Suzan Beraza captures the heated debate around a proposed uranium mill in Naturita, Colorado, following in the tradition of other nuanced environmental documentaries like **Gasland** (2010) and **Harlan County, USA** (1976). The film's strength lies in its refusal to take sides, instead highlighting how desperate communities sometimes face impossible choices between potential health risks and economic survival.

sections.content: The film connects thematically to other documentaries examining the impact of energy industries on small towns, like **GasLand Part II** (2013) and **The Overnighters** (2014). These works share a focus on how energy boom-and-bust cycles create both opportunity and devastation in rural communities. Beraza's approach echoes Barbara Kopple's landmark **Harlan County, USA** (1976) in its intimate portrayal of working-class families facing difficult choices about their community's future.

The visual language of **Uranium Drive-In** draws power from its use of the decaying drive-in theater as a metaphor for the town's economic decline. This technique recalls similar approaches in **Rich Hill** (2014) and **The Last Picture Show** (1971), where physical locations become powerful symbols of rural American transformation. The film's exploration of nuclear issues also connects it to dramatic features like **The China Syndrome** (1979) and documentaries like **Containment** (2015). SUBHEAD: Environmental Documentary Evolution

The film represents an important evolution in environmental documentary filmmaking, moving beyond simple activist narratives to explore more complex territory. Like **If You Build It** (2013) and **The Biggest Little Farm** (2018), it shows how environmental and economic concerns often create seemingly irreconcilable conflicts in small communities. This approach contrasts with earlier environmental documentaries like **An Inconvenient Truth** (2006), offering a more nuanced view of how environmental issues affect real communities.
